newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy reform commission enters final phase.
newsitem.headline: Italy reform commission enters final phase.

text.p: The work of Italy's all-party parliamentary commission on constitutional reforms enters a new phase on Wednesday when its chairman outlines proposals to give Italy stable government and effective law-making.

Massimo D'Alema, head of the ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), will sum up progress to date by four sub-commissions and raise the curtain on the next and most delicate phase -- voting on proposals in coming weeks.
Political sources said D'Alema would propose a compromise solution between conflicting demands from the centre-left and the centre-right on what reforms should be enacted.

One of the key issues in the so-called bi-cameral commission, set up in February, is whether Italy's president and prime minister should be elected directly by the people. The commission has six more weeks to complete its work.
Italian presidents are elected by parliament and they in turn appoint prime ministers after consulting political parties.
Centre-left forces, who are currently in power, back a proposal whereby Italian parties making up electoral coalitions would identify their candidate for prime minister before national elections.
Thus, Italians voting for parliamentarians in electoral coaltions would indirectly choose the prime minister.
Centre-left parties also want the prime minister be given more executive authority, such as the power to dissolve parliament in case of a vote of no-confidence in a government.
Under the current constitution, parliaments are dissolved by the president, who then calls early elections.
The centre-right parties want Italy's president to be elected directly by the people instead of by parliament and to have a more direct role in government decisions.
Reform of Italy's 1948 constitution is one of the toughest political challenges facing the country, which has had 55 governments since World War Two.
There have been three general elections since 1992 in the upheavals that followed the exposure of entrenched political corruption and the collapse of the old governing class.
Two previous attempts to change the way Italy works have failed in the past 15 years and deep differences divide the opposing blocs on the best blueprint for reform.
There were indications that the separtist Northern League, which withdrew its six members from the commission in February to press demands for federalist reform, may re-join for the final phase.
League leader Umberto Bossi was due to meet D'Alema for talks before the commission chairman made his recommendations.
The League, which has declared a symbolic independent northern "republic", has demanded an option of a referendum on secession.
Federalist reform and tax decentralisation have been the sujbect of one of the sub-commissions but its report is not complete.
The 70-member commission is also considering streamlining parliament, whose two existing houses duplicate each other's functions.
It must report back to parliament by the end of June. Both houses are then expected to spend a year studying proposals and drawing up a package of changes to put to a referendum.
